quiz.q: How does Cargo treat each `.rs` file placed directly under `tests/`?
options: As a module inside your library crate
As its own separate crate, compiled and linked against your library
As a script that's ignored unless named `main.rs`
As documentation, not code
quiz.explain: Every file directly under `tests/` is compiled as its own independent binary crate that depends on your library, the same way an external project would.

quiz.q: Why does `tests/api.rs` write `use my_crate::add;` instead of `use super::*;`?
options: It's just a style preference, both work identically
Because it's a separate crate, not a child module of your library — there is no `super` to reach through
`use super::*` is deprecated
Because integration tests can't use the `use` keyword
quiz.explain: `tests/api.rs` is compiled as its own crate, so it imports your library the way any external dependency would — by crate name, not by `super`.

quiz.q: What can an integration test in `tests/` NOT see that a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` unit test CAN?
options: Public functions
Private (non-pub) items
The standard library
println! output
quiz.explain: Integration tests are compiled as a separate crate and only see your `pub` API, just like any real external user of your library. Unit tests live inside the crate and can see everything.

quiz.q: Why do integration tests only work for library crates?
options: Binary crates don't support the `tests/` folder syntax
A binary crate produces no importable library artifact for a tests/*.rs file to `use`
Cargo forbids running `cargo test` on binaries
Integration tests require async code
quiz.explain: `use my_crate::...;` needs a compiled library (an rlib) to depend on. A `src/main.rs`-only project has no such library target.

quiz.q: What's wrong with naming a shared test helper file `tests/common.rs`?
options: Nothing, it's the recommended approach
Cargo treats it as its own separate test crate, so it runs (with zero tests) and shows up in the output
It causes a compile error
It's only a problem on Windows
quiz.explain: Cargo auto-discovers every direct child of `tests/` as its own test crate. `common.rs` gets run as a (nearly empty) test binary — harmless, but noisy and not what was intended.

quiz.q: How do you correctly share setup helpers across multiple integration test files?
options: Put them in `tests/common.rs` and import with `use`
Put them in `tests/common/mod.rs` and declare `mod common;` in each file that needs them
Copy-paste the helper code into every test file
Put them in `src/lib.rs` marked private
quiz.explain: Cargo only auto-discovers files directly inside `tests/`, not ones nested in a subdirectory — so `tests/common/mod.rs` is never treated as its own test crate. Each file opts in explicitly with `mod common;`.

quiz.q: A private helper function inside your library needs a direct test. Where should that test live?
options: In `tests/api.rs`, since integration tests are more thorough
It can't be tested at all
In a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` unit test inside the same file, which can see private items
In `tests/common/mod.rs`
quiz.explain: Integration tests only see `pub` items. A private helper needs a unit test inside the crate, where `use super::*` gives access to private internals.

quiz.q: What's a real cost of a large integration test suite?
options: It makes your release binary larger
Each file in `tests/` triggers its own full compile of your library, which can noticeably slow `cargo test`
It disables unit tests
It requires nightly Rust
quiz.explain: Because each `tests/*.rs` file is a separate crate, Cargo compiles your library against each one independently — many files means many compiles.

flashcards.front: How does Cargo compile files inside `tests/`?
flashcards.back: Every `.rs` file directly under `tests/` is compiled as its own separate crate, linked against your library exactly like an external dependency would be.

flashcards.front: What can integration tests see of your crate, and why?
flashcards.back: Only `pub` items — because each test file is a genuinely separate crate, it goes through the same visibility rules as any outside consumer of your library.

flashcards.front: Why do integration tests only apply to library crates?
flashcards.back: `use my_crate::...;` requires a compiled library artifact to depend on. A binary-only crate (no `src/lib.rs`) has no importable public API.

flashcards.front: What's wrong with `tests/common.rs` for shared helpers?
flashcards.back: Cargo auto-discovers it as its own test crate (with no tests in it), which is noisy and not intended — it shows up in `cargo test` output as a nearly-empty test run.

flashcards.front: What's the idiomatic way to share setup code across integration test files?
flashcards.back: `tests/common/mod.rs`, declared via `mod common;` in each file that needs it — files nested in a subdirectory of `tests/` aren't auto-discovered as their own test crates.

flashcards.front: Unit test or integration test: checking a private helper function directly?
flashcards.back: Unit test (`#[cfg(test)] mod tests` inside the file) — integration tests can't see private items at all.

flashcards.front: What real cost scales with the number of files in `tests/`?
flashcards.back: Compile time — each file is its own crate, so Cargo recompiles your library against every one of them.

flashcards.front: How would you fix a binary-only project (`src/main.rs`, no `src/lib.rs`) that wants integration tests?
flashcards.back: Move the logic you want tested into `src/lib.rs`, and make `main.rs` a thin wrapper that calls into the library.
